newsitem.title: USA: Northeast Utils CEO says recovery on track.
newsitem.headline: Northeast Utils CEO says recovery on track.

text.p: Top Northeast Utilities officials told shareholders Tuesday the troubled Connecticut-based utility's nuclear and financial recovery strategies are on track.

"While the past year and a half has been the most challenging in the history of the Northeast Utilities system, there are changes underway in the company that brighten our prospects for the future," Northeast Chairman and Chief Executive Bernard Fox said at the company's annual meeting.
Fox said the company was digging out of a financial hole and also working on a plan to face industry deregulation.
"We are working on parallel paths to assure that your investments are protected as the (electricity) industry is deregulated and to prepare our company for a competitive marketplace," Fox said.
Bruce Kenyon, chief executive of Northeast's nuclear operations, said the recovery schedule of the company's three Millstone nuclear power plants is "on track."

The three units, with an overall generating capacity of about 2,700 megawatts, have been shut since early 1996, forcing the company to buy electricity from independent power producers and other utilities to keep up with local demand.
Kenyon said he still expects to meet the recovery schedule for the units that was announced earlier this year.

"We are making progress that demonstrates clear success as we move down the road to restart of Millstone unit 3 late in the fourth quarter of this year, followed by unit 2, and finally unit 1," Kenyon said.
Actual restart dates hinge on approval by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission once it is satisfied Northeast has adequately dealt with safety concerns raised earlier at the Millstone facility.
Northeast chief financial officer John Forsgren said the company has taken steps to maintain access to liquidity while the expensive Millstone outages continue.

Those steps include suspending from March 25 payment of Northeast's common dividend, trimming internal budgets in some non-nuclear areas of the company, and entering new and improved financing arrangements.
Northeast has projected its costs related to the Millstone outages at about $990 million through 1998.
"These measures...are specifically designed to keep our cash flow healthy during this difficult period, and they are working," Forsgren said.

He said it is too early to determine when the company can resume dividend payments because two key issues are unresolved -- the restart of the Millstone units and regulatory uncertainties as Connecticut and New Hampshire, Northeast's main service territories, hammer out plans to deregulate their respective electricity industries.
The company also has not yet announced a successor to chief executive Bernard Fox, who said in February he plans to retire August 1.
